comparator.name: Culturele antropologie en ontwikkelingssociologie
comparator.sourceNotes: The degree has 75 EC of compulsory major study, 60 EC of major electives and 45 EC of profiling. The example uses the published 2026–2027 timetable and includes the usual second fieldwork course as a major elective. The 45 EC of profiling remains open subject to the level and approval rules.
components: Culturele antropologie 1: Inleiding in de culturele antropologie
Culturele antropologie 2: Sociale ordening en betekenis
Cultural Anthropology 3: History and Theory in Anthropology
Cultural Anthropology 4: Globalization and Sociocultural Complexity
Anthropology and Sustainability: Contemporary Fault Lines
Political Ecologies: Nature, Humans and Non-Humans

core: Cultural anthropology, social theory and comparative understanding of human societies
Culture, meaning, identity, belonging and everyday social life
Globalisation, migration, institutions, nationalism, conflict and power
Ethnographic fieldwork, qualitative methods, statistics and research writing
Diversity, inequality, exclusion and social development
Research ethics, reflexivity and representation of other perspectives
adjacent: Historical and material-cultural context for societies and identities
International relations, governance and transnational change
Human–environment relations and sustainability as fields of social change
questions: How can social problems be researched from people's own perspectives?
How do communities experience violence, security and conflict differently?
How do migration, identity and unequal power reshape societies?

alternatives.label: Culture, Society and Social Research
alternatives.labelReason: Social theory, cultural history and material culture supply the substantive core. Qualitative and quantitative courses support empirical inquiry.
alternatives.concept: Study how communities create meaning and organise social life. Combine social theory, cultural history and material culture with qualitative research and statistics.
progression: Introductory sociology precedes qualitative inquiry and modern social theory. Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory. Research Methods & Statistics adds empirical design and quantitative analysis.

alternatives.label: Migration, Identity and Inequality
alternatives.labelReason: Social theory, histories of empire and gender, rights, media and collective action illuminate identity and inequality.
alternatives.concept: Study how migration, empire and social institutions shape belonging. Use histories of race and gender, sociology, media and human rights to examine inequality and collective responses.
progression: Introductory sociology precedes qualitative inquiry and modern social theory. Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory.
alternatives.distinctness: This option gives greater weight to rights, migration, gender, representation and collective action, with dedicated historical and social-psychological perspectives.

alternatives.label: Global Change, Communities and Sustainability
alternatives.labelReason: Sustainability and environmental science support questions about how communities and institutions respond to global change.
alternatives.concept: Study how communities and institutions respond to global change. Combine social research, governance and environmental science to examine sustainability debates, collective action and policy.
progression: Sustainability foundations precede the advanced environmental course. Introductory and modern sociology precede advanced social theory. Qualitative inquiry and applied communication add complementary ways to study and engage communities.
alternatives.distinctness: This option adds sustainability, ecology, environmental processes and applied climate communication to the shared social-science core.

selection.assessment: Three defensible options retain different academic priorities: comparative culture and social research, identity and inequality, and global change and sustainability. Qualitative inquiry is common, while the closest option adds statistics and the global-change option adds applied sustainability communication. None reproduces the full anthropology and ethnographic fieldwork sequence.

notes.text: Utrecht has a dedicated ethnographic sequence from methods and research design to supervised fieldwork and a thesis written in pairs. UCR offers qualitative research, and the closest option adds research statistics. The UCR options draw on different disciplines to study related social questions.

audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s degree studies how people organise social life, create meaning and respond to change. It combines anthropological theory, social research methods, major electives and supervised ethnographic fieldwork.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options focus on culture and research, identity and inequality, or global change and sustainability. Utrecht provides a longer anthropology sequence and a dedicated progression from ethnographic design to fieldwork and thesis.

curriculum.limitation: This example shows eight compatible major electives, including extended fieldwork. The profiling choices remain open.

componentNotes.ca-bap-2: Complete the 45 EC of compulsory first-year courses and 75 EC of major electives or profiling before this course.
componentNotes.ca-bap-3: Pass BAP 1 and BAP 2 before beginning supervised fieldwork.
componentNotes.ca-choice-fieldwork: This example takes BAP 4 with BAP 3. Taking BAP 3 alone requires agreement with the coordinator.
componentNotes.ca-bap-thesis: Pass BAP 1, 2 and 3. Students write in pairs and receive individual assessments.
componentNotes.ca-profiling: Choose 45 EC, with at least 15 EC at intermediate level or above.
